title: Mixed Precision: FP32, FP16 & BF16
interviewAnswer: Mixed precision runs many expensive operations in FP16 or BF16 while keeping numerically sensitive parts at higher precision. It reduces memory bandwidth and often increases GPU throughput; BF16 has a wider exponent range, while FP16 may need loss scaling during training.
why: Mixed precision is one of the highest-leverage ways to fit larger batches/models and accelerate modern GPU workloads.
intuition: Use fewer bits where precision is not crucial, but protect calculations that would overflow/underflow or accumulate error.
deepDive: Automatic mixed precision chooses operation dtypes. FP16 has more mantissa precision than BF16 but much less exponent range; BF16 is often easier for training on supported hardware. Numerical validation remains essential.
workedExample: A model that uses 14 GB in FP32 may fit comfortably under mixed precision, allowing a larger batch and better GPU utilization without changing the architecture.
commonMistakes: Assuming half precision always produces identical numerics.
Using lower precision without checking hardware support or final quality.
followUps: Why can BF16 train without loss scaling more often?
Would you use mixed precision for CPU inference?
production: Track accuracy and latency/memory jointly; mixed precision can change kernel choice and numerical behavior across devices.

lab.goal: Use PyTorch autocast safely for inference and verify output shape/finite values.
lab.buildIt:
import torch
model=torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(128,256),torch.nn.ReLU(),torch.nn.Linear(256,10)).cuda().eval()
x=torch.randn(64,128,device='cuda')
with torch.inference_mode(), torch.autocast('cuda',dtype=torch.float16):
    y=model(x)
print(y.dtype,y.shape)
lab.useIt:
# Training usually combines autocast with GradScaler for FP16.
scaler=torch.amp.GradScaler('cuda')
